name: Vera Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Vera, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at the copper pit outside town, one of the big ones that carries about two hundred and twenty tonnes a load. I've been lead hand on our haul crew for nine years, so I'm the one who sorts out who goes on which truck, and I do the pre-start talk at six in the morning. Then it's ten or eleven hours of loop: down the ramp to the shovel, back up to the crusher, again and again. What I like is the quiet in the cab before dawn and knowing every pothole on that road. What wears me out is the nights on rotation, and my back after thirty-two years of bouncing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you know every pothole. What does a senior driver know that a new one doesn't?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: You know when the shovel operator is having a bad day from how he drops the load. You know the ramp gets greasy after the water truck goes past at nine, and you take it a gear lower. Last winter I caught a cracked rim on one of the young guys' trucks just from the sound it made idling. Thirty-two years and I can hear a cracked rim from across the go-line, but I've never once asked a computer a question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. At the union meeting I'd tell people the sky didn't fall and we should stop letting management scare us with it. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something from the union page about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, even if the clever computer stuff is hype, the driverless trucks aren't. They run them at the company's other pit already, two hundred kilometres north, and that's not AI hype, that's a machine on GPS. So for me, plateau or not, the trucks are still coming for my seat sooner or later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep my head down until sixty-five. I'd push harder on our next agreement for a clause that says nobody loses their job to automation without a redeployment offer and a proper payout. And I'd try to put a bit aside, maybe a hundred a fortnight, though that's hard on what they pay us out here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of relief, but not much. It's like hearing the storm turned away but you can still see it sitting on the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the other pit up north. What have you heard from people there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin's boy, Danny, drove there until two years ago. Now he sits in a room watching screens for six trucks at once, and he says half his old crew took the payout and left town. They didn't need AI to get rid of the drivers up north. They just needed GPS and a bean counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a hundred a fortnight is hard. What does the money look like at home right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon drives the school bus, so between us we get by, but we've still got four years left on the car loan. We helped our daughter with her rent bond last year and that took what little we had. If something big broke on the house tomorrow, it would go on the card.

S0.say: I'd tell the union meeting that the sky didn't fall and we should stop letting management scare us with AI. I'd share something from the union page about it online.
S0.think: Even if thinking AI is hype, the driverless haul trucks already run at the company's other pit and are not hype. She expects them to come for her seat whatever happens to AI.
S0.do: Keeps working and keeps her head down until sixty-five. Pushes in the next agreement for an automation clause with redeployment offers and payouts, and tries to save about a hundred every fortnight.
S0.feel: Some relief, but the worry about driverless trucks doesn't go away.
S0.quote: They didn't need AI to get rid of the drivers up north. They just needed GPS and a bean counter.
S0.fieldNote: Vera separates AI hype from the trucks she has already seen run without drivers, so a plateau barely changes her picture. Her first move is through the union, not through her own retraining. The thin savings came up quickly and concretely: a car loan and help with a daughter's rent bond.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what I always say: if the company makes more money with fewer people, the people should get a share of it. I'd be on the phone to the union organiser the first week. Online I'd probably share the petition, whatever it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, steady change is the one that gets me. It's slow enough that nobody makes a fuss, and fast enough that by the time I'm sixty-one there's no seat left for me. They'll take the trucks first because that's the easiest bit to automate, and I'm a truck driver, simple as that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and help write the claim for a transition deal, things like early retirement on full pension for anyone over fifty-five. I'd stop the extras at home, no takeaway, no new phone, and we'd sell the second pickup. I'd also write to our local representative in government, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. I feel like I'm being asked to clap while they pull the chair out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The company might offer to train drivers to supervise the driverless trucks from a control room. Would you put your hand up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let the young ones go first, honestly. I've never used a computer for more than the roster, and I'd be sitting in a room with screens, which isn't me. I'm good at one thing, which is driving that truck. Ask me to babysit six of them from an office and I'd be the worst one there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who's been with us three years and has two little ones, and she's a good driver. And old Ray, who's sixty-one and can barely read the rosters on his phone. I'd worry about Ray more than me, which tells you something.

S1.say: If the company makes more money with fewer people, the workers should get a share of it. She would call the union organiser in the first week and share the petition online.
S1.think: Steady change is the one that scares me, because it's quiet enough that nobody fights it and fast enough to take my seat before I'm sixty-one. Trucks are the easiest part to automate and I'm a truck driver.
S1.do: Helps write a union claim for early retirement on full pension for over-fifty-fives. Cuts takeaway and new phones, sells the second pickup, and writes to her local representative in government for the first time.
S1.feel: Tight in the chest, like she's being asked to clap while the chair is pulled away.
S1.quote: I'm good at one thing, which is driving that truck. Ask me to babysit six of them from an office and I'd be the worst one there.
S1.fieldNote: Vera sees steady change as more dangerous than it sounds, because it is quiet. She would not volunteer for control-room retraining and is frank that she would be bad at it. Her concern for colleagues like Ray and Priya is real and runs alongside her own fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in now, not after. There should be a law that a company can't throw a whole town away because a robot got cheap. I'd say that at the pub, at the union, wherever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, two years means I'm sixty when my seat goes. That's five years short of the pension, with less than a month in the bank. I don't think I'd find another job in this town, because the mine is the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ring the union and ask what the redundancy terms really are, in writing. I'd go to the welfare office and find out what we'd get, because I've never needed to know. We'd cut back to the bone and Gordon would ask for more runs on the bus. If there's a protest at head office, I'm on the bus to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the ground's moving under the truck and I can't find the brake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do differently in those two years than with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's nothing to plan, you just grab what you can. I'd take every overtime shift going and put it all on the car loan so at least that's gone. With five or ten I could think about it; with two I'd just be bracing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our son not to worry, because that's what you say. Then I'd ring my daughter and ask if her landlord would take a pet, because if we lose the house we'd need somewhere for the dog. That's the part that would get me, asking my own daughter where the dog could go.

S2.say: The government needs to step in now, with a law that stops a company throwing a whole town away because robots got cheap. She would say it at the pub and the union alike.
S2.think: Two years means losing her seat at sixty, five years short of the pension, with less than a month saved. The mine is the town, so she sees no other job to go to.
S2.do: Gets the redundancy terms in writing through the union and finds out what welfare she would get. Takes every overtime shift to pay off the car loan, cuts spending to the bone, and joins any protest at head office.
S2.feel: Sick, like the ground is moving under the truck and she can't find the brake.
S2.quote: That's the part that would get me, asking my own daughter where the dog could go.
S2.fieldNote: Two years leaves Vera with nothing to plan, only bracing, and she said so directly. She admitted she has never needed to know what welfare would pay. The moment about asking her daughter where the dog could go carried more feeling than anything about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for anyone, the company or the government, to be caught napping. The union should be at the table from day one. I'd say that on the union page and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three. That's close enough to the pension that I might just scrape through, or I might miss by two years and that's the difference between being all right and selling the house. It's a coin toss, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with the union's pension adviser and work out the earliest I could go without losing half of it. I'd ask the company straight out for a date when the trucks go driverless, so I can plan to it. Every spare bit of money would go to clearing the car loan first, then a small buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sick than the last one. It's a countdown, but at least I can see the numbers on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years instead of two change for you, practically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me finish paying the car off and maybe help Gordon get his heavy rigid licence, so he can drive trucks on the road, not just the bus. With two years I'm bracing. With five I'm counting, and counting's better than bracing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never sit in the control room. Would five years change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if they trained us on the clock and paid us while we learned, I'd sit beside someone for a few months and see. I still don't think I'd be good at it. But I'd rather say no to something real than to something I've only heard about.

S3.say: With five years' warning there's no excuse for the company or the government to be caught napping. The union should be at the table from day one.
S3.think: Five years puts her at sixty-three, so she might just reach the pension or miss by two years. That gap is the difference between being all right and selling the house.
S3.do: Sees the union's pension adviser to find the earliest safe retirement date and asks the company for the date the trucks go driverless. Pays off the car loan first, builds a small buffer, and helps her partner get a heavy truck licence.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier than with two years, because she can see the numbers on the countdown.
S3.quote: With two years I'm bracing. With five I'm counting, and counting's better than bracing.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Vera's panic into arithmetic about her pension date, which she finds easier to hold. She shifted slightly on control-room work, but only if paid training came first, and she still doubts herself. Her plan leans on her partner's earning power as much as her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so let's do it properly: retraining paid by the company, pensions protected, no town left behind. I'd say we shouldn't let them waste the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years and I'm sixty-eight, so by then I'm on the pension and out of it. My worry would be the young ones on my crew, and the town. But for me personally, it's the one I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much changes in my first year, I'll be honest. I'd keep driving, keep paying down the loan, and work on the union's transition committee so there's a plan for the people coming after me. I'd plan to go at sixty-five like I always meant to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay for me, a bit guilty about that. And sad for the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You feel safe with ten years. What would worry you about how the town uses that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone goes to sleep for eight of the ten years. That's what happened when the smelter closed in the nineties: everyone knew it was coming and nobody did anything until the gates were locked. Ten years is a gift, and this town has a habit of leaving gifts in the wrapping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want said at your send-off, when you leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I never left anyone on the ramp. That I fought for the young ones even when I was going out the door myself. I don't need a gold watch, just that.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to do it properly, with company-paid retraining, protected pensions and no town left behind. She would say they must not waste the decade.
S4.think: By 2036 I'll be sixty-eight and on the pension, so this is the one I can live with. My worry is for the young ones on my crew and the town.
S4.do: Keeps driving and paying down the car loan, and joins the union's transition committee to plan for younger workers. Plans to retire at sixty-five as she always intended.
S4.feel: Mostly okay for herself and a bit guilty about that, and sad for the town.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift, and this town has a habit of leaving gifts in the wrapping.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Vera's fear shifts from herself to her crew and the town. She remembers the smelter closing in the nineties and fears the same drift. Her guilt about feeling safe was striking and honest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because I'd be out at sixty with nothing behind me. What would help is a bridge to the pension: if they pay older workers through to sixty-five when the robots come in, I'd go quietly. And the union having a real seat at the table, not a seat at the back.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the bodies. Thirty-two years in a truck and my back and knees are shot, so a lot of us would be glad not to drive. The robots taking the job isn't the problem. Taking the pay with it is.

headlineQuote: Thirty-two years and I can hear a cracked rim from across the go-line, but I've never once asked a computer a question.
portrait: Vera Zhang is a 58-year-old lead hand on the haul truck crew at a large copper pit, with thirty-two years in the cab and almost nothing saved. She is a union woman who has never asked a computer a question and doesn't intend to start. A plateau barely reassures her, because driverless trucks already run at her company's other pit. Two years' warning leaves her panicked about losing her seat at sixty with no pension, while ten years lets her reach sixty-five and turn her worry towards her crew and her town.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she would lose her job at sixty, five years short of her pension, with less than a month of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Pay that bridges older workers to sixty-five when the robots come in, and a real union seat at the table.
